cf.title: LWLock granular partition lock memory layout

input.subject: LWLock granular partition lock memory layout

verdict_reasoning: The proposal fails at level 1b on evidence. demand-1: message #3 asked for numbers from realistic workloads, and message #4 says the effect is not visible on one on the author's machine. already-exists-1: the thread never compares the patch with unpatched Postgres that has S times more padded partitions, which costs a few KiB. The idea may be sound, but the list needs both answers before design review.

brief.title: Pack several partition LWLocks into one cache line
brief.problem: Partitioned hash tables in shared memory use an array of LWLocks, each padded to a full cache line to avoid false sharing. The author argues that the same memory could hold more partition locks, giving more concurrency and less contention. The thread does not name a workload or user that suffers from the current layout.
brief.proposed_design: Patch 0001 declares the main LWLock partition groups as struct fields so offsets come from the struct layout instead of recursive macros, without changing allocation. Patch 0002 adds an LWLockAligned type smaller than LWLockPadded, sized as a divisor of the cache line, so S partition locks share one cache line. Individual (unpartitioned) LWLocks keep full padding.
user_visible_surface: New LWLockAligned type in storage/lwlock.h, visible to extensions using the C API.
Changed declaration of partition lock groups in lwlocklist.h, lock.h and buf_internals.h, which code computing partition lock offsets may depend on.
Changes in pg_config_manual.h; the material does not say which setting is added or changed.
author_claims: Packing S partition locks per cache line raises LW_EXCLUSIVE concurrency by about a factor S, with no added cache-line traffic per operation.
It reduces contention on LWLockWaitListLock, CAS retries in LWLockAttemptLock, and the number of backends that sleep.
"In theory this has benefits with no compromises."
pgbench on an 8-core laptop with 128 partitions: about 26% more throughput at 8 clients, no change at 1 client.
The author expects larger gains on multi-socket machines but did not measure them.
brief.thread_state: Nathan Bossart asked for numbers from realistic workloads and could not tell what benchmark.txt shows. The author replied with one pgbench result at 1 and 8 clients; no one has replied to it.
unclear: The material does not say which partitioned locks change: buffer mapping, lock manager, predicate lock, or all of them.
The pgbench script, scale, mode (read-only or read-write) and number of runs are not stated in the thread.
The material does not say whether the number of partitions changes, or only the memory layout.
The value of S, the cache line size assumed, and behaviour on platforms with other cache line sizes are not given.
There are no results for exclusive-heavy workloads, where locks sharing a cache line may cause more false sharing.
The material does not say what changes in pg_config_manual.h or whether extensions using these lock arrays must change.

prior_attempts.title: Cache line alignment of PGXACT
prior_attempts.quote: It became clear that this patch causes regression.
prior_attempts.reason: Benchmarks showed read-only gains but regressions on read-write and mixed workloads, and the author judged the read-write loss about as large as the read-only gain. The author also found that padding PGPROC, or another unrelated alignment change, gave the same read-only effect, so it was unclear the patch itself was needed. The author returned the patch for more investigation.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P6 added cache-line alignment to PGXACT entries; this proposal reduces padding of partition LWLocks. P6 supports only the request for read-write runs and a layout control.

objections.title: No user or workload shown to suffer from padded partition locks
objections.failure_scenario: A committer changes the layout of shared lock arrays, the buffer mapping and lock manager locks among them, based on one laptop pgbench run. No user has reported contention on these locks, so nothing shows that anyone in the field gains. If the multi-socket gain never appears, the project keeps the extra layout complexity for nothing.
objections.argument: In message #3 Nathan Bossart asked for numbers from realistic workloads. In message #4 the author says the effect cannot be seen on a realistic workload on the test machine and only expects it on multi-socket hosts. Message #5 gives one run at 1 and 8 clients, without the script, scale, mode or which partitioned locks changed. The thread has no field report, no wait-event data and no second person asking for this.
objections.author_must_show: On which production-like workload and hardware do partition LWLock waits show up in pg_stat_activity wait events, and how much does the patch reduce them?

critic.reasoning: Message #4 says the effect is not visible on a realistic workload on the author's machine, and the thread has no field report or wait-event data. The single pgbench result in message #5 shows a gain but not a user who needs it.

objections.title: Raising the existing partition-count constants may give the same gain
objections.failure_scenario: A committer compares the patch with a one-line change to LOG2_NUM_LOCK_PARTITIONS or NUM_BUFFER_PARTITIONS, which keeps every lock on its own padded cache line. If that matches the 26% gain, the project has added a second LWLock layout type and a new struct layout for a few KiB of shared memory.
objections.argument: Partition counts are already compile-time constants in lwlock.h. The author's model compares S packed locks against one padded lock, but the plain alternative is S padded locks on S cache lines, which has no false sharing. With 128 partitions that alternative costs about 8 KiB more per S step. Message #5 compares patched against base at the same count and never against base with S times more partitions.
objections.author_must_show: With the same pgbench run, how does the patch compare with unpatched Postgres where the partition count is raised by a factor of S, and what is the memory difference?

critic.reasoning: The thread compares patched against base only, never against base with S times more padded partitions, which costs a few KiB. [P6] is about PGXACT alignment and must not be used as support here.

other_surviving.title: Layout-only gain shown on one workload, read-write and exclusive cases unmeasured
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A committer pushes the packed layout on the strength of a laptop pgbench gain. On a write-heavy many-core server, backends taking LW_EXCLUSIVE on neighbouring partition locks keep pulling the same cache line between sockets. Throughput drops, and users find out only after upgrading.
other_surviving.argument: [P6] changed the cache-line layout of a shared-memory array and saw read-only gains with read-write regressions. In that thread an unrelated alignment change gave the same read-only effect. The tight loop in benchmark.txt takes only LW_SHARED, and message #5 does not give the pgbench mode, scale, number of runs or partition set. Message #4 says realistic workloads showed no effect on the author's machine, so the 26% figure could be an alignment artifact of the kind [P6] reported.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What do read-write and exclusive-heavy pgbench runs show on a multi-socket machine, and does an unrelated layout change reproduce the 26% gain?

critic.reasoning: The benchmark.txt loop takes only LW_SHARED, and message #5 gives no pgbench mode, scale or run count. [P6] concerns a different structure, so it supports only the request for read-write runs and a layout control.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Second lock stride makes partition offsets easy to get wrong
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An extension or a later core patch computes a partition lock address as MainLWLockArray plus an offset, assuming LWLockPadded stride. After this change the code still compiles, but it can lock the wrong partition or memory inside another lock. The error appears only as rare corruption or hangs under concurrency.
other_surviving.argument: Patch 0001 changes how partition groups in lock.h, buf_internals.h and lwlocklist.h are declared, and 0002 adds LWLockAligned next to LWLockPadded. Each new partitioned lock group must then choose a stride, and the build does not complain when code uses the wrong one. The proposal does not say how existing users of the offset macros are kept working, or whether they must change.
other_surviving.author_must_show: What stops code that indexes the main lock array with the old stride from compiling silently, and which extension-visible macros keep their meaning?

critic.reasoning: The material does not say whether the old offset macros remain or what type the main lock array keeps, so the silent-compile case cannot be ruled out. Code using the partition lock accessor macros would follow the change, which limits the exposure to direct offset arithmetic.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Packed partition locks add cross-partition cache line traffic under write load
refuted.failure_scenario: On a many-core or multi-socket server, backends take LW_EXCLUSIVE on different buffer mapping or lock manager partitions that now share one cache line. Each atomic operation on one lock invalidates the line for the others, so throughput drops under write-heavy load. Users see this only after upgrade, with no setting to turn it off.
refuted.argument: The 0002 commit message shows that traffic per cache line does not depend on S when the number of cache lines is fixed. But the current layout has one lock per line, so the same partition count would use fewer lines and lines would bounce more. The only results are a shared-only tight loop and one pgbench run at 1 and 8 clients on a laptop, with the script and mode not stated (message #5). In [P6], a cache line layout change helped read-only pgbench but regressed read-write, and that patch was returned.
refuted.author_must_show: How do read-write and exclusive-heavy workloads behave on a multi-socket machine with the patch, compared with raising the partition count while keeping padded locks?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 for the unmeasured exclusive-heavy case and of already-exists-1 for the comparison with more padded partitions. Its extra-traffic claim assumes fewer cache lines, but the 0002 commit message describes the same memory holding more locks.

refuted.title: Cost lands on all users and extensions, gain is unmeasured
refuted.failure_scenario: Every installation gets the new packed layout for partition locks, and extensions that compute partition lock offsets must follow the new struct declarations. On an exclusive-heavy workload, backends that take different locks on one shared cache line contend, and throughput drops. Users find this only after upgrading, because only shared-heavy loops and one pgbench run were measured.
refuted.argument: The change is not opt-in, so the risk falls on everyone while the claimed gain is mostly expected on hardware nobody tested (message #4). The benchmark.txt loop takes LW_SHARED only. In [P6], a cache-line layout change gave read-only gains but read-write regressions about as large, and the patch was returned. Message #5 claims "benefits with no compromises" but shows no write-heavy or mixed results.
refuted.author_must_show: What are the results on read-write and exclusive-heavy workloads, on at least one many-core or multi-socket machine, with the script and run count stated?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 for the unmeasured write-heavy risk and of maintenance-fit-2 for the extension cost. The who-pays framing also fits poorly, because a layout change that is not opt-in gives any gain to all users too.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: Patch 0002 adds LWLockAligned to lwlock.h, and 0001 changes partition lock declarations in lock.h, buf_internals.h and lwlocklist.h.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A second lock stride sits next to LWLockPadded, and each future partitioned lock group must choose one.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Partition LWLocks, which sit on the lock acquire and release path, would share cache lines.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Raising the existing compile-time partition counts with padded locks may give the same gain.

questions: On which realistic workload and hardware do partition LWLock waits show up in wait events, and how much does the patch reduce them?
With the same pgbench run, how does the patch compare with unpatched Postgres whose partition count is raised by a factor of S, and what is the memory difference?
What were the pgbench script, scale, mode and number of runs behind the 26% result at 8 clients?
Which partitioned locks change (buffer mapping, lock manager, predicate lock), and does the number of partitions change or only the memory layout?
What do read-write and exclusive-heavy runs show on a multi-socket machine, where locks on one cache line may cause false sharing?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the LWLock code and the layout of the main lock array. The one reviewer in the thread only asked for numbers.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the performance of the buffer mapping and lock manager partition locks on all hardware, including multi-socket machines that nobody measured, for every later release.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted a corrected patch one day after the first and answered the request for numbers with a pgbench result.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: Repeatable results on a many-core or multi-socket machine, with script, scale, mode and run count stated, for read-only and read-write loads. They must show a gain over both unpatched Postgres and unpatched Postgres with S times more padded partitions.

priority.reason: The patches are small, but they change the layout of core lock arrays, and judging them needs benchmark work on large machines. The thread shows one laptop pgbench result and no workload that suffers today, so review time is better spent once the measurements exist.

provisional_note: Without the code, the change in pg_config_manual.h, the value of S and the fate of the old offset macros are unknown. The level 2 objections on exclusive-heavy false sharing and on the second lock stride were not evaluated.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Don't lock partitions pruned by initial pruning"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Don't lock partitions pruned by initial pruning"
Reverted commit(s): Ensure first ModifyTable rel initialized if all are pruned
precedents_retrieved.objection:
As pointed out by Tom Lane, the patch introduced fragile and invasive
design around plan invalidation handling when locking of prunable
partitions was deferred from plancache.c to the executor. In
particular, it violated assumptions about CachedPlan immutability and
altered executor APIs in ways that are difficult to justify given the
added complexity and overhead.

This also removes the firstResultRels field added to PlannedStmt in
commit 28317de72, which was intended to support deferred locking of
certain ModifyTable result relations.

precedents_retrieved.title: Delay locking partitions during query execution
precedents_retrieved.summary: Skip locking partitions in AcquireExecutorLocks() and lock each one only when the executor first opens it in ExecGetRangeTableRelation(), so that partitions removed by run-time pruning are never locked. The patch adds a delaylock flag to RangeTblEntry, and the main gain is for prepared statements that use generic plans over many partitions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it after he found a cached generic plan that fails with "could not open relation with OID" when another session drops an index on a partition that was not locked. Robert Haas had said the patch is dead unless the executor can cope with arbitrary AEL-requiring changes to delay-locked partitions. The only fix the author saw was to take partition locks on the top-level partitioned table, which is a larger, separate change. Tom Lane also objected to storing planner output in RangeTblEntry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If you can't,
then this patch is dead.

This reverts commit ec386948948c and its fixup 589bb816499e.

This change was intended to support query planning avoiding acquisition

precedents_retrieved.title: Lazy JIT IR code generation to increase JIT speed with partitions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch delays JIT IR generation until an expression is first executed, so plan nodes that never run, such as most Parallel Append children over many partitions, are never compiled. A later version also cached the to-be-inlined bitcode modules and cloned them with llvm::CloneModule() instead of reloading them from disk.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that lazy generation emits roughly one module per function, which is inherently more expensive than emitting one module per query. He would not accept a one-function-per-module design as the base for usage-triggered JIT. He also warned that IRMover renames types in cloned modules, which can degrade code quality. David Geier then found that the module cache had stopped inlining altogether, and that cloning early made llvm::CloneModule() so slow that JIT time stayed high, so he stopped work on it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think that's just inherently more expensive and thus a no-go.

precedents_retrieved.title: Cache line alignment of PGXACT
precedents_retrieved.summary: Align each PGXACT entry in shared memory to a cache line, or to 16 bytes in a later version, so that entries do not share or straddle cache lines. The goal was to cut contention and raise pgbench -S throughput on machines with many cores.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks showed read-only gains but regressions on read-write and mixed workloads, and the author judged the read-write loss about as large as the read-only gain. The author also found that padding PGPROC, or another unrelated alignment change, gave the same read-only effect, so it was unclear the patch itself was needed. The author returned the patch for more investigation.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It became clear that this patch causes regression.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert an ill-considered portion of my patch of 12-Mar, which tried to save a few lines in sql_exec_error_callback() by using the function source string...
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert an ill-considered portion of my patch of 12-Mar, which tried to save a few lines in sql_exec_error_callback() by using the function source string field that the patch added to SQL function cache entries.  This doesn't work because the fn_extra field isn't filled in yet during init_sql_fcache(). Probably it could be made to work, but it doesn't seem appropriate to contort the main code paths to make an error-reporting path a tad faster.  Per report from Pavel Stehule.

field that the patch added to SQL function cache entries.  This doesn't work
because the fn_extra field isn't filled in yet during init_sql_fcache().

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix pg_rewind false positives caused by shutdown-only WAL
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes how pg_rewind finds the end of WAL on the target, so that a shutdown checkpoint written after the divergence point does not by itself make a rewind necessary. pg_rewind would scan backward from the last checkpoint to the last record that is not shutdown-related.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas objected to the premise. The shutdown checkpoint updates the control file, and that change matters when deciding whether servers are in sync. Even if pg_rewind ignored those records, the restarted old primary still refuses to follow the new timeline. He also noted that the patch did not skip the RUNNING_XACTS record and did not check the rmgr ID, and he saw no workaround; a later patch from another poster got no reply before the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: But I do not think we can do that, because (1) those WAL records might do important things like update the control file and (2) the server will not be OK with ignoring those WAL records even if pg_rewind decides that they are not important.

precedents_retrieved.title: XLog size reductions: Reduced XLog record header size
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patchset makes the WAL record header variable-length, which shrinks it to 14-21 bytes, with about 4-5% less WAL estimated for pgbench. It varlength-encodes the record length, gives rmgrs their own info byte, includes the XID only when the record asks for it with XLOG_INCLUDE_XID, and adds an invalid rmgr ID 0 used to detect the end of WAL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding after review. Michael Paquier objected to the opt-in XLOG_INCLUDE_XID interface and questioned the use of rmgr ID 0 as an end-of-WAL marker. Pavel Borisov then asked for benchmarks showing the gain was large enough, the benchmarking was still a todo, and a reminder from Andrey M. Borodin in April 2024 got no visible reply before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But at the second round, some doubt arises on whether this long
patchset indeed introduces enough performance gain?

precedents_retrieved.title: hashjoin - gracefully increasing NTUP_PER_BUCKET instead of batching
precedents_retrieved.summary: When the hash table for a hash join does not fit in work_mem at the initial NTUP_PER_BUCKET load factor of 1, the patch tries load factors of 2, 4 and 8 before falling back to batching. If batching becomes necessary at run time, it switches back to the default load factor, and explain shows the load factor.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author's own tests showed that even a load factor of 2 was slower than going to two batches when temp files stay in the page cache; only an outer table large enough to cause real I/O favoured the higher load factor. Kevin Grittner could not build a case where the change won and judged that detecting the cases where it would help would be hard and add cost to every hash join. No one found a reliable way to detect those cases, so the author asked to mark it rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The patch was meant as an attempt to implement Robert's idea
from the hashjoin patch, but apparently we have no clear idea how to do
it without hurting performance for many existing users.

precedents_retrieved.title: Optimize numeric comparison and aggregation via packed-datum extraction
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch speeds up numeric min, max, sum, avg and variance by reading numeric fields directly from packed (1-byte header) datums, so that each row no longer needs a detoast with palloc and memcpy. min and max return the original input Datum, and the accumulation functions use a new init_var_from_packed().
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Only the author posted: a v2 patch fixed a CFBot alignment failure on strict architectures, and no reviewer reply appears in the thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert workarounds for -Wmissing-braces false positives on old GCC
precedents_retrieved.authors: Peter Eisentraut, Michael Paquier, Andres Freund
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert workarounds for -Wmissing-braces false positives on old GCC
Reverted commit(s): Drop warning-free support for Flex 2.5.35; Silence -Wmissing-braces complaints in file_utils.c; Attempt to fix compiler warning on old compiler; Attempt to fix compiler warning on old compiler; Try to silence "-Wmissing-braces" complaints in rmgrdesc.c.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
We have collected several instances of a workaround for GCC bug 53119,
which caused false-positive compiler warnings.  This bug has long been
fixed, but was still seen on the buildfarm, most recently on lapwing
with gcc (Debian 4.7.2-5).  (The GCC bug tracker mentions that a fix
was backported to 4.7.4 and 4.8.3.)

That compiler no longer runs warning-free since commit 6fdd5d95634, so
we don't need to keep these workarounds.  And furthermore, the
consensus appears to be that we don't want to keep supporting that era
of platform anymore at all.

This reverts the following commits:

d937904cce6a3d82e4f9c2127de7b59105a134b3
506428d091760650971433f6bc083531c307b368
b449afb582bb9015bfbb85abc10ce122aef9ec70
6392f2a0968c20ecde4d27b6652703ad931fce92
bad0763a4d7be3005eae35d460c73ac4bc7ebaad
5e0c761d0a13c7b4f7c5de618ac38560d74d74d0

and makes a few similar fixes to newer code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Reducing serialized size of Nodes from nodeToString output
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set shrinks the text form of pg_node_tree written by nodeToString by about half. It omits fields with zero or curated "default" values, drops query-text locations, trims trailing zeroes in outDatum, and run-length codes bitmapsets and integer lists.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut committed only the ParseLoc type and the change that makes nodeToString drop location fields. He held back the rest because omitting fields and compact list coding save storage but make debug node dumps harder to read, and other reviewers gave little feedback. He also noted that no one had measured the effect on (de)serialization performance, and that saving a few hundred KiB of view storage did not justify the change alone.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think to proceed we need more buy-in on the "what do I want from my
node dumps" side, and more performance numbers on the other side.

roaster_notes.note: P16 shares the contention topic but records no reason, so it supports nothing here. The thread does not point to any earlier discussion of packing partition locks.

The proposal changes only the shared-memory layout of partition LWLocks, with no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object, dump content or client-visible behaviour, so nothing in the standards and compatibility angle fails. Changing the C-level lock array declarations is normal in a major release; whether extensions that index MainLWLockArray directly must change, and what pg_config_manual.h gains, cannot be checked without the code.

The proposal changes only the shared memory layout of partition LWLocks, which is rebuilt at every server start. It touches no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, replication path or wire protocol, so pg_upgrade and standbys are unaffected. Extensions that index MainLWLockArray directly with the partition offset macros may need source changes in a major release. That is normal for master-only changes, and the material does not show such a dependency.

The proposal changes only the shared-memory layout of partition LWLocks. It adds no SQL surface, privilege, role, setting reachable by users, monitoring view or authentication path, so no new action or information becomes available to a non-superuser. False sharing between packed locks is a performance question for other panel members, and it gives an unprivileged user no denial-of-service path beyond the lock contention ordinary queries already cause.
Two objections apply from this angle. No committer who knows the LWLock area has engaged beyond asking for numbers, but that is a committability point and not counted as an objection.
One objection from this angle. No extension or hook covers LWLock memory layout, so the only existing alternative is raising the partition-count constants.
